title: The first sin
hook: Augustine taught that Adam's guilt is inherited; the Orthodox speak of inheriting mortality and a wounded nature, not guilt

segments.voice: Yesterday, image and likeness: the image given to every person, the likeness grown into. Your line was image given, likeness grown. Did the quality you picked show itself? Day one thousand seventy-six.

Why is it so easy to do the very thing you just decided not to do? The second cookie. The sharp reply. The phone, picked up again. Paul knew the problem. In his letter to the Romans, in the King James Bible, he writes: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Christian readers have heard more than a bad day in it: something in the grain of being human, a pull that's there before anyone chooses it. Christians have a name for where that pull comes from, and they tell the story behind it in more than one way. Today's word: original sin.
screen: `THE THING YOU DECIDED NOT TO DO.`
`THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.`

segments.voice: Original sin doesn't mean an unusual sin. It means the sin at the origin: Adam and Eve in the garden, reaching for the fruit, and everything that followed. Paul ties the story to all of us in Romans: "as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." Christian teaching, East and West, says something went wrong at the start and reached everyone. They differ on what exactly was passed down. Augustine, the bishop in North Africa, taught that Adam's guilt itself is inherited: in Adam, all of humanity sinned, and every child is born sharing that guilt as well as its damage. In the Western churches, Catholics and Protestants build on his reading, in different ways and with different stresses. The Orthodox churches of the East tell it differently. What we inherit from Adam, they say, is not his guilt. It's mortality, and a wounded nature that leans toward sin. A newborn isn't guilty of anything. But that newborn is born into a world where death and the pull toward wrong are already in the air. So guilt, in Orthodox teaching, is for sins a person actually commits. Here's what both readings refuse to say: that a person is worthless. Before the garden, Genesis says God looked at everything he had made, "and, behold, it was very good." The fall doesn't undo that. Wounded, in every telling. Worthless, in none. The wound is real. So is the very good.

Here's the practice: notice the pull toward wrong in you. Settle, and breathe. Don't hunt for your worst moment. Just think back over the last day, and find one small place where you felt a tug in a direction you didn't want to go. Impatience. A little lie. Wanting to be first. Look at it the way a doctor looks at a bruise: honestly, without disgust. Name it to yourself, quietly. If you pray, you can hold it out to God and ask for healing. If you don't, just let it be seen, and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Original sin. The sin at the origin, and what it left in us. Augustine said guilt; the Orthodox say mortality and a wounded nature.
Your line: wounded, not worthless. Today, when you catch the pull again, name it, and then say the other half to yourself: very good, from the start. Day one thousand seventy-six.

howItsDone: Christians speak of original sin when they teach about baptism and grace; Western churches build on Augustine's teaching of inherited guilt in different ways, while Orthodox churches teach that people inherit mortality and a wounded nature, not Adam's guilt.

original.note: Latin: original sin, the sin at the origin. A Western phrase, associated with Augustine.

what it means: the sin at the origin left a wound in everyone; churches differ on whether guilt is inherited too.

notes: The Orthodox position (inherited mortality and a corrupted or wounded nature, not personal guilt) is summarized; confirm with an Orthodox Keeper. Romans 5:12's 'for that all have sinned' is read differently East and West (Augustine's Latin 'in quo', in whom); left out under the claims rule.

'In the Western churches, Catholics and Protestants build on his reading, in different ways' is a general historical claim; confirm. Catholic teaching speaks of original sin as 'contracted, not committed'; Reformed teaching stresses inherited guilt more. Not detailed here.
The 'original' note associates the Latin peccatum originale with Augustine; confirm he used the phrase (e.g., Ad Simplicianum 1.1.10) or drop the association.
Practice invites noticing without self-contempt; confirm it is suitable and does not assume the listener's beliefs.
Editor: Paul's line is no longer stated to describe a pull before choice; that reading is attributed to Christian readers. 'The churches agree' softened to 'Christian teaching, East and West, says'.
